text: Frogs are in trouble around the world. In 2023, a huge study by hundreds of scientists found that about 41% of all known kinds of [[amphibian|amphibians]] are at risk of extinction. Amphibians are the group that includes frogs, toads, salamanders and newts.

Several things are hurting them at once. Ponds and forests are being drained and cleared. A deadly fungus has spread across continents. The [[@climate-change|climate]] is getting hotter and drier in many places. And [[pesticide|pesticides]] and other chemicals wash into the water where frogs lay their eggs.
Frogs are easy to harm because they live two lives, first as tadpoles in water and then as adults on land. Damage either home, and they suffer.

st.prompt: Frogs breathe partly through their skin. Why does that make them extra sensitive to pollution?

options.t: Chemicals in water and air pass easily through their thin skin
Pollution makes their skin change colour so predators see them
Their skin is too thick for chemicals to escape

st.reveal: A frog's skin is thin and damp so that oxygen can pass through. Unfortunately, pesticides and other chemicals can pass through just as easily, so frogs are often among the first animals to suffer when a pond or stream gets polluted.

d.try: On a rainy evening, sit quietly with an adult near a garden, park or field and listen for frogs. Try to count how many different calls you hear, such as croaks, chirps, whistles or clicks. Each kind of frog has its own call. If you can, record a few seconds on a phone to compare on another night.
myth: Touching a toad gives you warts.

Warts on people are caused by a virus that spreads between humans, not by toads. The bumps on a toad's skin are glands. Some toads make a poison that can irritate your eyes or mouth, so wash your hands after handling one, but it won't give you warts.

sec.t:
Most frogs lay jelly-covered eggs in water. These hatch into tadpoles, which breathe with gills and nibble on [[algae|algae]]. Over weeks or months they grow legs, lose their tails and change into frogs. This change is called [[metamorphosis|metamorphosis]].

So a frog needs clean water to breed and damp land or trees to live in. If a pond is filled in to build houses, or a stream dries up, the frogs that depend on it can vanish.

Frogs also breathe partly through their thin, moist skin. That lets oxygen in, but it lets pollution in too. Scientists sometimes treat frogs as an early warning: when frogs disappear, something is often wrong with the water or the land.

In the 1990s, scientists in Australia and Central America found frogs dying in clean, protected rainforests. The cause turned out to be a [[fungus|fungus]] called chytrid. It attacks the skin, stopping frogs from taking in water and salts properly.

Chytrid seems to have spread from East Asia, probably carried around the world by the trade in frogs as pets and food. A 2019 study linked it to the decline of about 500 amphibian [[species|species]], with around 90 thought to have died out completely.

One victim is the Panamanian golden frog, a bright yellow frog that was a national symbol of Panama. It has not been seen in the wild for years. Some survive in zoos and breeding centres, where scientists hope one day to return them to the forest.

{{story:extinction-today}}

India is a frog hotspot. The [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] alone are home to well over 200 kinds of amphibians, most found nowhere else on Earth. New species are still being discovered almost every year.

Some are very unusual. The purple frog is fat and round with a pointy nose. It lives underground, eats termites and comes up only for a few days in the [[monsoon|monsoon]] to breed, joining the [[@frogs-monsoon|rainy-season chorus]] of other frogs. Indian dancing frogs live by fast forest streams. Since the noise of rushing water drowns out their calls, the males wave their legs to show off to females.

Many of India's frogs live in small patches of forest. When those patches are cleared for farms, roads or plantations, a species can be wiped out before anyone has even named it.

Around the world, people are fighting back. Scientists keep backup populations of rare frogs in zoos, and test treatments for chytrid. Volunteers in the UK and USA help toads and salamanders cross busy roads on rainy spring nights.

In India, researchers and nature groups run frog-watching walks during the monsoon and encourage people to record frog calls. Schools build small ponds without fish, which give tadpoles a safe home. Protecting [[@wetlands|wetlands]], streams and patches of forest is the best help of all, because frogs need both water and land to survive.

text: People have called the mango the king of fruits for centuries, especially in India, and it is easy to see why. A ripe mango is sweet, juicy and fragrant, and there are hundreds of varieties, each with its own taste. Mango trees grow huge, live for a century or more, and give shade as well as fruit.

The mango is also deeply woven into Indian life. It has been grown in India for over 4,000 years. It appears in poems, paintings and festivals, and mango leaves are strung over doorways on happy occasions.
Today India grows more mangoes than any other country, roughly two in every five mangoes on Earth, and the mango is India's national fruit.

st.prompt: How do growers make sure a new mango tree gives exactly the same fruit as a favourite old tree?

options.t: They plant a seed from its best mango
They join a cut twig from the old tree onto a young seedling
They water it with the same well water

st.reveal: A mango seed grows into a tree whose fruit can be quite different from its parent's. So growers use grafting, joining a twig from a favourite tree onto young roots. The twig grows into a copy of the original, which is how varieties like Alphonso and Dasheri stay the same.

d.try: Collect a few different mangoes in season, or look carefully at pictures if you can't. Compare their shape, skin colour, smell near the stalk, and how soft they feel when gently pressed. With an adult, cut them open and taste. Make a table and give each one a score.
myth: A mango's colour tells you whether it is ripe.
Many varieties stay green or only partly yellow when ripe. A gentle squeeze and a sweet smell near the stalk are better clues than colour.
facts: South and Southeast Asia, around northeast India and Myanmar

sec.t:
Wild mangoes grow in the forests around northeast India, Bangladesh and Myanmar. The wild fruit is small and stringy. Over thousands of years, people chose and planted the trees with the best fruit, slowly turning it into the mango we know.

A mango tree can grow over 30 m tall, about as high as a ten-storey building, with a wide, dark-green crown. Some trees in India are well over a hundred years old and still bear fruit. [[@buddha|The Buddha]] is said to have rested in mango groves, and one grove was given to him and his followers as a gift.

India has over a thousand [[@mango-varieties|named mango varieties]]. Alphonso, from Ratnagiri and Devgad in Maharashtra, is famous for its saffron flesh. Dasheri comes from Malihabad near Lucknow. Langra, Chausa, Kesar from Gujarat, Banganapalli from Andhra Pradesh and Himsagar from Bengal all have loyal fans.

Most varieties are kept going by [[grafting|grafting]]: joining a cutting from a favourite tree onto young roots. Portuguese settlers in [[@goa|Goa]] helped spread grafting in India from the 1500s, and the Alphonso is widely said to be named after the Portuguese general Afonso de Albuquerque.

In Malihabad, a farmer named Haji Kalimullah Khan has grafted around 300 varieties onto a single old tree. He was awarded the Padma Shri in 2008.

{{story:akbar}}

The Mughal emperors loved mangoes. Emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] is said to have planted an orchard of a lakh mango trees near Darbhanga in Bihar, known as the Lakhi Bagh. Mughal gardens across north India had mango groves for shade and fruit.

Poets praised the mango too. In [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poetry, including the works of [[@kalidasa|Kalidasa]], mango blossoms announce the arrival of spring and are linked with Kama, the god of love. The curved paisley shape found on many [[@textiles-india|Indian fabrics]] is often called *ambi*, meaning "little mango".

Mangoes reached the Americas with Portuguese and Spanish traders, and today they grow in Mexico, Brazil and Florida. For years, the USA banned Indian mangoes because of worries about pests. In 2007, after a trade agreement, the first Alphonsos were shipped to America, treated to make sure no insects came along.

Mangoes also play a part in friendship between countries. Leaders in South Asia sometimes send boxes of their best mangoes to one another as gifts, a habit people jokingly call mango diplomacy. It is one small part of [[@trade-world|world trade]].

The mango belongs to the same plant family as cashews, pistachios and poison ivy. Its sap and skin contain a substance that can cause an itchy rash in some people, especially around the mouth. If that happens to you, it's best to let an adult peel and slice the fruit.

In the hot weeks of summer, mangoes are everywhere in India: in aam panna, aamras with puris, [[@pickles-achar|pickles]] and lassi. The season is short, but people wait all year for it.

text: Termite mounds work less like an air conditioner and more like a pair of [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]]. A big termite colony, with up to millions of insects, uses up a lot of oxygen and makes a lot of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. The termites live mostly in a nest at the bottom, and the tall tower above it helps fresh air get in and stale air get out.

The trick depends on the Sun. During the day, the thin outer walls of the mound warm up faster than the thick middle, so air moves one way. At night, the outside cools first, and the air moves the other way. This daily swing keeps air flowing through the mound, a bit like breathing.
The walls are full of tiny holes, so gases can seep through without letting rain, [[predator|predators]] or dry wind in.

st.prompt: What do mound-building termites grow in gardens inside their nests?

options.t: Grass
A fungus
Tiny plants that need no light

st.reveal: The termites collect dead plants, chew them and pack the mush into spongy combs. A fungus grows on the combs and breaks the tough plant matter down. The termites then eat the fungus and the softened food.

Turner J.S. (2000) The Extended Organism. Harvard University Press.

n.certNote: Mounds clearly help move air in and out of termite nests. How exactly they do it, and how steady they keep the temperature, has changed as scientists measured more carefully, and may differ between species.

d.try: On a warm afternoon, stand in a closed room and hold one hand near the floor and the other as high as you can reach. If you have a thermometer, check both spots. The air up high is usually a little warmer, because warm air rises. Termite mounds use rising and sinking air like this to swap stale air for fresh.
myth: Termites are a kind of white ant.
Termites are often called white ants, but they aren't ants at all. Their closest relatives are cockroaches. Termites and ants just happen to have evolved similar busy colonies.
facts: worker termites, using soil, spit and droppings
mostly in the nest at the base, not the tower

sec.t:
Most termite workers are blind and smaller than a grain of rice. They build with soil, mixed with spit and droppings, carrying it grain by grain. No termite has a plan of the whole mound. Each one follows simple rules, like dropping soil where others have dropped soil, and the shape grows from millions of tiny actions.

The results can be huge. In parts of Africa, mounds tower over 5 m, taller than a double-decker bus. If termites were as tall as people, their mounds would be taller than the world's highest [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]].

Many mound-building termites are farmers. Workers collect dead leaves, grass and wood, chew it and pack it into spongy combs in special chambers. A [[fungus|fungus]] grows on the combs, breaking down tough plant matter that the termites couldn't digest alone. The termites eat the fungus and the softened food.

After the first [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains, this fungus sometimes pushes up through the mound as tall, pale [[@mushrooms|mushrooms]]. In parts of India, from Kerala and Odisha to the northeast, people gather them as a seasonal treat.

In Harare, the capital of Zimbabwe, the [[@jobs-architect|architect]] Mick Pearce designed an office and shopping building called the Eastgate Centre, opened in 1996. Inspired by termite mounds, it uses thick walls, chimneys and night-time breezes to stay cool without ordinary air conditioning. It uses much less energy than similar buildings.

Scientists now know the real mounds work a little differently from the original idea, but the lesson still stands. Nature had worked out clever cooling long before the [[@refrigerator|fridge]].

In northeast Brazil, there are about 200 million termite mounds spread over an area about the size of Great Britain. Some are around 4,000 years old, built by termites digging out tunnels and piling up the soil.

In India, termite mounds appear in tradition too. The poet Valmiki, who is said to have composed the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], is often linked to the Sanskrit word *valmika*, meaning a termite mound. A popular story says he meditated so long that a mound grew over him. In parts of South India, people offer prayers at termite mounds, which are believed to be homes of serpent spirits, and snakes do often shelter in old mounds.

text: DNA is a very long [[molecule|molecule]] inside your [[cell|cells]]. It carries the instructions for building and running your body, written in a code of just four chemical "letters": A, T, C and G. The order of the letters spells out the instructions.
Your DNA has about 3 billion pairs of letters. Printed as books, it would fill a big library shelf.

A section of DNA that holds the instructions for one job is called a [[gene|gene]]. Humans have about 20,000 genes that carry recipes for [[protein|proteins]], the building blocks and tiny machines of your body.

st.prompt: How many different 'letters' does DNA use?
st.reveal: DNA uses just four letters, A, T, C and G. Their order spells out instructions, just as computers use only 0 and 1.

d.try: Build a paper DNA ladder. Cut strips of four colours of paper for A, T, C and G, and glue them as rungs between two long paper strips, always pairing A with T and C with G. Write a secret word using your own colour code, then give a friend one side of the ladder and see if they can rebuild the other side.
myth: Your DNA decides everything about you.

DNA affects many things, such as your eye colour and blood group. But food, health, the place you grow up and the things you learn and practise shape you too. Even identical twins with almost the same DNA grow into different people.

sec.t:
DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder, called a *double helix*. Each rung is a pair of letters: A always pairs with T, and C with G. In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick worked out this shape, using [[@x-rays|X-ray]] pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin.

Franklin's sharpest picture, known as Photo 51, was shown to Watson without her knowing. She died in 1958, aged 37. Watson, Crick and her colleague Maurice Wilkins won the Nobel Prize in 1962, and today many scientists argue her part was not fairly recognised at the time.

All people share about 99.9% of their DNA. The tiny differences help make each of us unique. You got half your DNA from each parent, which is why you may have your mother's nose and your father's laugh.

We also share a lot with other living things. DNA is how scientists know [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds are dinosaurs]] and that [[mammoth|mammoths]] were closest to Asian elephants. Identical [[@twins|twins]] start with almost exactly the same DNA, because they grow from one fertilised egg that split in two.

In 1984, the British scientist Alec Jeffreys made a discovery. A few stretches of DNA vary so much between people that they can identify a person, a bit like a [[@fingerprints|fingerprint]]. Police soon began using this *DNA fingerprinting* to solve crimes and free people who had been wrongly jailed.

In India, the [[biologist|biologist]] Lalji Singh developed DNA fingerprinting methods at the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology in Hyderabad. It's now used in Indian courts and to reunite lost children with their families.

In 2003, scientists from many countries finished the Human Genome Project. They had read nearly all the letters of human DNA, a job that took 13 years and cost billions of dollars. Today a person's whole DNA can be read in about a day, for a tiny fraction of that cost.

DNA uses four letters. Computers use just two: 0 and 1. Both store huge amounts of information in long strings. Scientists have even stored books and short films inside man-made DNA, because a few grams of it could in theory hold more data than a whole room of computers.

text: Look closely at a train wheel and you'll see that its rolling surface isn't flat like a car tyre. It slopes slightly, so [[@wheel-invented|the wheel]] is wider on the inside, near the middle of the train, and narrower on the outside. Two such wheels are fixed firmly to one axle and turn together.

If the train drifts to the left, the left wheel rolls on its wider part and the right wheel on its narrower part. The wider wheel covers more ground in each turn, so the axle steers back to the right. Drift right, and the opposite happens. The wheels keep nudging themselves back to the centre.
Each wheel also has a lip, called a flange, on its inside edge. It catches the rail if something goes badly wrong. On a good track, though, the cone shape does nearly all the work.

st.prompt: On a curve, the outer wheel of a train has to travel further than the inner wheel. But they are fixed to the same axle and spin together. How does the outer wheel keep up?

options.t: The train shifts outwards, so the outer wheel rolls on its wider part
The outer wheel skids along the rail
The outer rail is made of a slippier metal

st.reveal: Because the wheels are cone-shaped, a slight shift outwards puts the outer wheel on its wider part and the inner wheel on its narrower part. A wider wheel covers more ground in each turn, so the pair naturally steers around the bend.

Lay two metre rulers or straight sticks side by side as rails, slightly apart, and roll your cups along them. They stay on, even round a gentle bend. myth: The lips on train wheels are what keep trains on the track.
The flanges are a safety backup. The cone shape of the wheels does almost all the steering, keeping the train centred and guiding it round curves without the flanges grinding against the rails.

sec.t:
On a curve, the outer rail is longer than the inner one. A car solves this with a clever set of gears that lets its wheels spin at different speeds. A train's wheels can't, because they are joined by a solid axle.

The cone shape solves it. As the train enters a curve, it shifts slightly outwards. Now the outer wheel rolls on its wider part and the inner wheel on its narrower part. In one turn of the axle, the outer wheel travels a little further, exactly as needed. The wheels correct themselves so eagerly that, at high speed, they can overshoot and make the carriage sway gently from side to side. Engineers call this hunting, and they design springs and dampers to calm it.

Engineers also tilt the track on curves, with the outer rail slightly higher, so trains lean into the bend like a cyclist.

The gap between the two rails is called the gauge. Much of the world, including the USA and most of Europe, uses standard gauge, 1,435 millimetres. Most Indian railway lines use a wider broad gauge, 1,676 millimetres, which allows bigger, steadier carriages.

[[@hist-first-train-india|India's first passenger train]] ran on 16 April 1853, from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, about 34 kilometres. It had 14 carriages pulled by three steam locomotives. Today [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]] carries more than 2 crore passengers a day.

sec.h: Mountains, toys and the circle trick
sec.t:
Not every train runs on a wide track. [[@india-wonder-toy-train|The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway]], nicknamed the Toy Train, runs on rails just 610 millimetres apart. It climbs steep hills using loops and zigzags, and it is a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site.

The cone-wheel trick works everywhere, from toy trains to giant freight trains. It comes down to a simple fact about [[@circles|circles]]: a bigger circle covers more ground in one turn than a smaller one. In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], [[@india-wonder-mumbai-local|the local trains]] use the same idea thousands of times a day, round every curve between Churchgate and Virar.

text: Gond art is a style of painting by artists from the Gond community, one of India's largest [[indigenous|indigenous]] or Adivasi groups. Gond families live across central India, especially in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]], Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra.

A Gond painting usually shows animals, trees, gods and stories from the forest. The shapes are bold and often bright, and their insides are filled with tiny repeated marks: dots, dashes, curves and scales. These patterns make a still picture feel as if it is shimmering. Most of the famous painters come from Patangarh, a small village in Dindori district.

st.prompt: What fills the inside of most animals and trees in a modern Gond painting?

options.t: Patterns of tiny dots, dashes and lines
Realistic fur and shading

st.reveal: Gond artists draw a bold outline, then fill it with repeating marks such as dots, short dashes, fish scales or wavy lines. Each artist develops their own filling pattern, almost like a signature.

myth: Gond art is an ancient style that has always looked the way it does today.

Gond people have decorated walls and floors for a very long time, but the detailed paintings on paper and canvas seen in galleries began in the 1980s. Today's style is a living art that keeps changing.

shapes filled with dots, dashes and lines

sec.t:
For generations, Gond women decorated the mud walls and floors of their homes, especially for festivals. They used white clay, coloured earth and charcoal. The designs faded with the rains and were painted again.

Among the Gonds are the Pardhans, a community of bards. They sang the stories of Gond gods and heroes, playing a stringed instrument called the *bana*. Those songs gave painters a huge store of characters and tales. Gond paintings often show a single moment from a story that everyone in the village already knew.

A typical Gond painting begins with an outline. Then the artist fills it with a filling pattern, repeated hundreds of times. One painter might use fish scales, another tiny seeds, another fine parallel lines. Experts can often tell who made a painting just from the pattern.

The patterns do more than decorate. Many artists say they show movement, sound or life inside a creature: ripples in water, wind in leaves, the energy of an animal about to leap. Because there is no shading or [[@perspective|perspective]], every part of the picture looks equally important, from the smallest insect to the biggest tree.

Trees appear again and again, especially the mahua and the [[@banyan|banyan]], which matter in Gond life and belief. Animals like the [[@tiger-stripes|tiger]], deer, peacock and fish are favourites. Sometimes the pictures surprise you: a tree's roots become snakes, or a bird turns out to be made of leaves.

Gond artists have also become well-known book illustrators. In 2004, Bhajju Shyam, who had trained with Jangarh, published *[[@kipling-india|The London Jungle Book]]* with Tara Books in [[@chennai|Chennai]]. It shows his first trip to London, painted in Gond style, with the city's buses and clocks turned into creatures of the forest.

Bhajju Shyam, Durga Bai Vyam and Ram Singh Urveti later painted *The Night Life of Trees*, which won a prize at the [[@book-fairs|Bologna Children's Book Fair]] in Italy. Bhajju Shyam and Durga Bai Vyam have both received the Padma Shri. Their work now hangs on museum walls in Bhopal and sits on bookshelves far from the forests that inspired it.

text: Singing starts in your voice box, or [[larynx|larynx]], the bump at the front of your throat. Inside are two small bands of tissue called vocal folds. When you breathe out and start to sing, the folds come together and air from your lungs makes them buzz, very fast.

To sing higher, small [[@muscles|muscles]] stretch the folds longer, thinner and tighter. Tight, thin folds vibrate faster, and faster [[vibration|vibrations]] make a higher note. It works like a rubber band: stretch it more and pluck it, and the note rises. Trained singers learn to control these tiny muscles very finely, while keeping a steady flow of air.

st.prompt: What actually vibrates to make the sound when you sing?

options.t: Two folds of tissue in your voice box
Your lungs
Your tongue

st.reveal: Air from the lungs passes between your vocal folds and sets them buzzing. The lungs supply the air and the tongue and lips shape the sound, but the folds make it.

src: Sundberg J. (1987) The Science of the Singing Voice. Northern Illinois University Press.

d.try: Rest your fingers gently on the front of your throat and hum a low note. Slowly slide up to a high note and feel the buzzing change. Then hum while you pinch your nose shut. The hum stops, because humming sends air out through your nose.
myth: Opera singers can easily shatter glasses with their voices.

It is possible but very hard. It needs a thin crystal glass, a very loud voice, and the exact note at which that glass naturally rings. A singer did it on an American TV science show in 2005, but it is not something singers do every day.
facts: vocal folds in the larynx, or voice box
about 100–120 vibrations a second for men, about 200 for women
Queen of the Night's top note

sec.t:
Every sung note needs air, supplied by your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]]. Singers practise breathing low and deep, using the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, the [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], along with the muscles of the belly and ribs.

The aim is a steady, controlled stream of breath, not a big gust. Long notes need careful saving of air. A singer holding a note for fifteen seconds is like a cyclist pedalling steadily uphill, not sprinting.

Very high notes need the folds to be stretched tight and to vibrate in only part of their length. A soprano's high C vibrates about 1,000 times a second.

In [[@mozart|Mozart]]'s opera *The Magic Flute*, the Queen of the Night sings a furious song that climbs to an F above that, about 1,400 vibrations a second. Few singers can perform it well. Above the normal range, some singers can reach a thin, piercing sound called the whistle register.

Trained [[@opera|opera singers]] also learn to make a strong ring in their voice, which helps them be heard over a whole [[@orchestra|orchestra]] without a [[@microphones|microphone]].

Indian classical singers do *riyaz*, daily practice, often early in the morning. One famous [[@exercise|exercise]] is *kharaj* practice: singing very low, steady notes to build breath and control. Singers also practise sliding smoothly between notes.

Playback singers in Hindi films have sung in huge ranges. [[@lata-mangeshkar|Lata Mangeshkar]] was known for a light, clear, high voice that she kept for decades. Singers in Carnatic music practise fast runs of notes called *brigas*, which need very quick, precise control of the vocal folds.

Vocal folds are delicate. Shouting for a long time, or singing hard when you have a cold, can make them sore and swollen, and your voice goes croaky. Most of the time, they recover with rest.

Singers drink water, warm up gently and avoid straining to reach notes. If someone's voice stays hoarse for weeks, it is a good idea to see a doctor. A well-cared-for voice can last a lifetime. Some singers keep performing into their eighties.

text: A government is the group of people and organisations that run a country, state or town. It makes rules, called laws, that everyone must follow. It runs services people share, like roads, schools, hospitals and the army. It collects [[@taxes|taxes]] to pay for them, and it keeps order through police and courts.

Different countries pick their governments in different ways. In a [[@democracy-what|democracy]] such as India or the USA, citizens choose their leaders by voting, and leaders must follow a [[@constitution|constitution]]. In other places, kings, the army or a single party hold power. Either way, someone has to decide how a country is run.

The Prime Minister alone

st.reveal: A new law must be passed by both houses of Parliament and signed by the President. The Prime Minister and ministers propose many laws, and the Supreme Court can strike down laws that break the Constitution, but neither makes laws alone.

sec.t:
Most [[democracy|democracies]] split government power into three parts, so no single person or group has too much.

The legislature makes laws. In India it is [[@parliament-india|Parliament]], with the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. In the USA it is [[@congress-usa|Congress]], with the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The executive carries laws out and runs the government day to day. In India, this is led by the Prime Minister and ministers. In the USA, it is led by the President.

The judiciary, the courts, settles disputes and decides whether laws and actions follow the [[constitution|constitution]].

A French writer called Montesquieu argued for separating these powers in 1748, and the idea shaped both the US and Indian constitutions.

A big country can't be run from one office. India's government has three levels. The Union government in New Delhi handles defence, money, railways and foreign affairs. Each [[@governors-states|state government]] runs its own police, hospitals and most schools. Local governments, [[@panchayat|panchayats]] in villages and municipalities in towns, look after water, drains, streetlights and local roads.

The USA works in a similar way: a [[federal|federal]] government in Washington, D.C., 50 state governments, and counties and cities below them.

Governments get most of their money from taxes. Workers pay income tax, shoppers pay GST or sales tax on things they buy, and companies pay tax on their profits. Each year India's Finance Minister presents a [[@budget-government|budget]] to Parliament, explaining how much the government plans to collect and spend.

When a government spends more than it collects, it borrows. How much to tax, spend and borrow is one of the biggest arguments in politics everywhere.

Because governments are powerful, democracies build in ways to watch them. Voters can remove leaders at the next election. Courts can cancel laws that break the constitution. [[@newspapers|Newspapers]] and TV report what leaders do. Citizens can protest peacefully and ask questions. In India, the [[@right-to-information|Right to Information Act]] of 2005 lets any citizen ask a government office for information, and it must reply within 30 days.

Even a small thing, like a broken streetlight, is the government's job. Many cities now let people report problems online, and a crew is sent to fix them.

text: When you drop a letter in a post box, it starts a relay. A postal worker collects it and takes it to a sorting office. There it is grouped with other letters going the same way, packed into bags and sent by van, train or plane. Near the end, a local post office sorts it once more, and a postman or postwoman carries it to your door.

The secret to all this sorting is the code at the bottom of the address. In India it is the six-digit PIN code. In the USA it is the five-digit ZIP code. Each number narrows the destination down step by step, the way a country, then a state, then a town would.

st.prompt: An Indian PIN code has six digits. What does the first digit tell the post office?

options.t: Which large region of India the letter is going to
How heavy the letter is
The street number of the house

st.reveal: India is split into eight geographic postal zones numbered 1 to 8, and 9 is used for the Army Postal Service. The next digits narrow it down to a sorting district, and the last three point to the exact delivery post office.

myth: The US Postal Service's official motto is "Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night..."
The Postal Service has no official motto. Those words are carved on a big post office building in New York City and come from an ancient Greek writer, Herodotus, describing Persian messengers.

sec.t:
India introduced the Postal Index Number, or PIN, on 15 August 1972. The first digit names one of eight large regions. Delhi, for example, starts with 1, and Kerala with 6. The second digit picks a smaller area, and the third a sorting district. The last three digits identify the exact post office that will deliver the letter.

The USA started ZIP codes in 1963. ZIP stands for Zone Improvement Plan. Its first digit also marks a big region, from 0 in New England to 9 on the West Coast. Without these codes, a sorter would have to know thousands of town names by heart.

In big sorting centres, machines now do much of the work. A camera photographs each envelope, and software reads the address, even many handwritten ones. The machine then prints a pattern of tiny lines on the envelope, a kind of [[@barcodes|barcode]], so later machines can sort it in a blink.

{{story:barcodes}}

Letters that the computer can't read go on screen to a human, who types in the code. In India, many letters are still sorted by hand into rows of pigeonholes. For more than a century, mail travelled in special carriages on [[@indian-railways|India's railways]], where clerks sorted it while the train rolled through the night.

At the end of the line, a postman or postwoman walks or rides a fixed route called a beat. Many know every house on it, which helps when an address is incomplete. Letters that can't be delivered or returned go to a special office, where staff open them to look for clues.

Until 1840, posting a letter in Britain could be expensive, and the person receiving it often had to pay. Then the Penny Black appeared, the first sticky postage stamp. Senders paid one penny in advance for a letter anywhere in the country. Other countries soon copied the idea. India's first stamps for the whole country came out in 1854.

In 1874, countries set up the Universal Postal Union so that mail could cross borders smoothly. A stamp from India pays for a letter's whole journey, even when another country's postman delivers it.

India Post has about 1.65 lakh post offices (2025), and about nine in every ten are in villages. Many are tiny, run from one room. Srinagar has a post office on a houseboat on Dal Lake. At Hikkim in Himachal Pradesh, about 4,400 m up, one of the world's highest post offices sends postcards from the snowy Spiti valley.

Post offices also do much more than mail. Many Indian families keep savings accounts there, and pensions and parcels pass across the same counter. In 2025 India Post introduced DIGIPIN, a code for any small square of land in the country. It could help find homes that have no street name at all, a problem [[@maps-grids|maps and grids]] have long tried to solve.

text: Code is a set of exact instructions, and computers can only follow instructions written in numbers and [[@logic|logic]]. So maths turns up everywhere in [[@programming|programming]]. Positions on a screen are coordinates. A score in a game is a variable, the same idea as x in algebra. Deciding whether to open a door uses logic: if the player has the key, then open.

You do not need advanced maths to start. Most beginner programs use counting, adding, comparing and repeating. But as programs get more ambitious, from 3D games to weather forecasts, the maths gets deeper too.

st.prompt: In code, the remainder when a number is divided by 2 is used to check something. What?

options.t: Whether the number is even or odd
Whether the number is positive or negative
Whether the number is bigger than 100

st.reveal: Any whole number divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 0 if it is even and 1 if it is odd. Programmers use this to colour every other row of a table, make a light blink or take turns in a game.

Most beginner coding uses counting, simple arithmetic and logic. Coding often makes maths easier to understand, because you can see numbers move things on a screen. Harder maths matters for some jobs, like graphics, AI or security.

sec.t:
Inside a computer, everything is stored as [[@binary-code|binary]], long strings of 0s and 1s. A letter, a photo, a song and a cat video are all numbers in the end. The letter A, for example, is stored as 65, which in [[binary|binary]] is 1000001.

Each [[pixel|pixel]] on your screen has numbers for how much red, green and blue light to show. A photo from a phone has millions of [[@pixels|pixels]], so even a simple filter, like making a picture brighter, means doing arithmetic millions of times in a blink.

Programs make decisions all the time. If the password is correct, open the home screen. If the ball touches the edge and the score is under ten, bounce. These rules use Boolean logic, named after George Boole, an English mathematician who worked in Ireland in the 1800s. In Boolean logic, every statement is either true or false, and words like and, or and not combine them.

Boole never saw a computer. But in the 1930s, an American engineer named Claude Shannon showed that electrical switches could do Boole's logic. Every chip in your phone is built from billions of tiny switches doing it.

One small operation is surprisingly useful: the remainder. In many [[@coding-languages|coding languages]] it is written with the % sign. Seven % 2 gives 1, because 7 divided by 2 leaves 1. If a number % 2 is 0, the number is even.

Programmers use remainders to make clocks wrap from 59 seconds back to 0, to colour every other row of a table and to share turns fairly between players. Loops, which repeat instructions, work hand in hand with them. A loop with a counter can draw a star, a spiral or a pattern of [[@tessellations|tessellating]] tiles in a few lines.

In 1843, Ada Lovelace, a young English mathematician, translated an article about [[@charles-babbage|Charles Babbage]]'s planned Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer. She added long notes of her own, including a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate a tricky sequence of numbers. It is often called the first published computer program.

[[@ada-lovelace|Ada Lovelace]] also guessed that such machines might one day make music or art, not just sums. She was right. Today, maths in code paints the animated films you watch and sorts the search results you see. Coding classes in schools from Bengaluru to Boston now use it to make maths feel like play.

text: Different places celebrate New Year on different days because they use different calendars. Most of the world uses the Gregorian calendar for everyday dates, so 1 January is a holiday almost everywhere. But many cultures also keep older calendars based on the Sun, the Moon or both, and each has its own New Year.

In India alone, people celebrate Ugadi, Gudi Padwa, Vaisakhi, Vishu, Puthandu, Pohela Boishakh, Navroz and more, at different times of year. Chinese communities celebrate Lunar New Year in January or February. Even 1 January itself arrives at different moments around the world, because of [[@time-zones|time zones]].

st.prompt: Which of these is the first inhabited place to welcome 1 January each year?

Tokyo, Japan
Sydney, Australia

st.reveal: Kiritimati, also called Christmas Island, is in the Line Islands of Kiribati, which uses the time zone furthest ahead on Earth. Its new year arrives about 14 hours before London's, and about eight and a half hours before India's.

myth: 1 January is the natural start of the year, chosen because something special happens in the sky.
Nothing special happens in the sky on 1 January. The date comes from Roman custom, and many cultures start their year at a new moon, a spring equinox or the harvest instead.
facts: start of the Gregorian calendar year

sec.t:
The Romans first named 1 January as the start of their year. In 46 BCE, Julius Caesar [[@calendar-maths|reformed the calendar]], and from 45 BCE the year began on 1 January. The month was named after Janus, a Roman god with two faces, one looking back and one looking forward.

Later, much of Christian Europe moved the start of the year to other days, such as 25 March. England kept 25 March until 1752, when it [[@oddity-calendar-missing-days|switched to the Gregorian calendar]] and to 1 January.

India has used many calendars, as [[@indian-calendars|India's calendars]] explains. Some follow the Moon and the Sun together, and New Year falls on the new moon of Chaitra, in March or April. That is Ugadi in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, and Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra, where families hang a decorated pole with a silk cloth and an upturned pot outside their homes.

Other regions use a solar calendar, and New Year falls around 14 April, when the Sun enters the sign of Aries. That is Vaisakhi in Punjab, Vishu in Kerala, Puthandu in Tamil Nadu, [[@art-bihu|Bohag Bihu]] in Assam and Pohela Boishakh in Bengal. Many Gujarati families celebrate New Year the day after [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]].

Nowruz, meaning "new day", is the Persian New Year, held at the spring [[equinox|equinox]] around 20 or 21 March. It is celebrated in Iran, Central Asia and by many communities elsewhere. In India, Parsis celebrate Jamshedi Navroz in March.

Many Parsis also celebrate another New Year in August. Their traditional calendar never added leap days, so over the centuries it drifted away from the seasons. A missing quarter-day each year, as [[@leap-years|leap years]] explains, adds up to months over a thousand years.

sec.h: The first and last to celebrate
sec.t:
The world is divided into time zones, so midnight on 31 December travels around the globe. The Line Islands of Kiribati, in the Pacific, are the first inhabited place to reach 1 January. Samoa and [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]] follow soon after, then Australia, Asia, Europe and the Americas.

India, at five and a half hours ahead of London, celebrates midway through the wave. In New York, a lit ball has dropped from a pole in [[@times-square|Times Square]] at midnight since 1907. The last inhabited places to enter the new year are American Samoa and nearby islands, about 25 hours after Kiribati.

text: When someone gets hurt, the first thing to do is stay calm and check that you're safe. Don't run onto a road or touch a broken wire to help. Then get an adult as fast as you can: a parent, a teacher or a nearby grown-up.

If it's serious, call for help. In India, the national emergency number is 112, and in most states 108 brings an ambulance. In the USA, it's 911. Tell them what happened and where you are. For small injuries, simple first aid makes a big difference: [[@water-purify|clean water]] for cuts, cool water for burns, and comfort for the person who is hurt. Being kind and staying with them matters more than you might think.

If you do call an emergency number, try to stay on the line and answer the questions slowly. The person on the phone is trained to guide callers, step by step, until help arrives. They may ask your address, what happened and whether the person is awake and breathing.

st.reveal: Leaning forward lets blood drip out instead of running down the throat, which can make people feel sick. Pinch the soft part just below the bony bridge for about 10 minutes without letting go. If it doesn't stop after 20 minutes, get help from an adult.

sec.t:
Most cuts and grazes are small. Rinse the cut with clean running water to wash out dirt. Then press on it with a clean cloth or tissue to stop the bleeding. Once it stops, a plaster or bandage keeps germs out while it heals.

Your body does a lot of the work itself. Blood thickens at the cut, and within a day a [[@scabs|scab]] forms to seal it. A deep cut, one that keeps bleeding or one made by something dirty or rusty needs an adult to check it, and maybe a doctor.

For a bump or a twisted ankle, rest the injured part. Hold something cold against it, such as an ice pack wrapped in a cloth. That reduces swelling and [[@pain|pain]]. The [[@bruises|bruise]] may change colour over the next few days as the body clears the blood under the skin.

For a [[@nose-bleeds|nosebleed]], sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes. Don't tip the head back. Any bang to the head that makes someone sleepy, confused or sick needs a doctor straight away.

In 1859, a Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant passed the battlefield of Solferino in northern Italy. Thousands of wounded soldiers lay there with almost no one to help. He organised local people to care for them, then wrote a book calling for trained volunteers in every country. This led to the founding of the [[@red-cross|Red Cross]] in 1863. Dunant shared the first [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 1901.

Today, the Red Cross and Red Crescent work in almost every country, and the Indian Red Cross Society dates from 1920. Many schools teach first aid, and organisations like St John Ambulance run classes for children. Knowing how to [[@telephone|call for help]] and what to say is the most useful first-aid skill of all.

text: Inside almost every cell of your body is a long [[molecule|molecule]] called [[@dna|DNA]]. It holds the instructions for building and running you, written in a chemical code. The instructions are divided into sections called [[gene|genes]]. Some genes help decide your height, the curl of your [[@hair-grow|hair]], the colour of your eyes and the shape of your nose.

You get two copies of each gene, one from your mother and one from your father. So you're a mix of both. But each parent passes on only half of their own genes, chosen by chance. That's why brothers and sisters look alike but not the same, and why you might have your grandmother's nose or your uncle's laugh.

st.prompt: Two brown-eyed parents have a baby with blue eyes. How is that possible?

options.t: Each parent carried a hidden gene for lighter eyes and passed it on
It isn't possible, so something must be wrong
Babies' eyes change colour depending on the weather

st.reveal: Each parent has two copies of each gene. A parent can have brown eyes while carrying a hidden version for lighter eyes. If both pass on the hidden version, the child's eyes can be blue. Eye colour is shaped by several genes, so families can surprise you.

It's rare but possible. Eye colour isn't controlled by one gene but by several working together, so the old simple rule taught in school doesn't always hold.

sec.t:
Your DNA is very long. Stretched out, the DNA in a single cell would be [[@body-weird-facts|about 2 metres long]]. To fit, it's coiled up tightly into 46 bundles called [[chromosome|chromosomes]], arranged in 23 pairs. In each pair, one came from your mother and one from your father.

When a parent's body makes an egg or a sperm cell, each pair is split up and shuffled, so only one of each pair goes in. Pieces of the two chromosomes can even swap places first. The result is that each egg and sperm carries a slightly different mix. The number of possible combinations is so huge that, apart from identical [[@twins|twins]], no two people have ever had the same set.

Some versions of a gene are dominant, which means they show up even if you have only one copy. Others are recessive, and they only show if you get two copies, one from each parent. A recessive version can hide for generations, then reappear when two carriers have a child.

Most traits, though, aren't controlled by a single gene. Height is shaped by hundreds. [[@eyes-colour|Eye colour]] depends on several, which is why [[@body-eye-colour-babies|brown-eyed]] parents can have a blue-eyed child, and occasionally the other way round. [[@blood-groups|Blood groups]] are one of the few traits that follow simple rules quite closely.

Genes give you a starting plan, but life shapes how it unfolds. Food, sleep, exercise, illness and the world around you all affect how tall you grow and how healthy you are. Identical twins share all their genes, yet they can turn out quite different.

In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick, using [[@x-rays|X-ray]] pictures made in Rosalind Franklin's lab, worked out that DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder. In 2003, scientists finished reading almost the whole human code for the first time. They found about 20,000 genes, far fewer than many expected. A water flea has more.

text: You grow taller because your long bones, like those in your legs and spine, get longer. Near each end of these bones is a thin layer of softer, rubbery tissue called [[cartilage|cartilage]]. This is the growth plate.

Cells in the growth plate keep dividing and piling up, pushing the ends of the bone further apart. Behind them, the older cartilage slowly hardens into bone. The whole process is driven by growth [[hormone|hormone]], a chemical messenger from a pea-sized [[gland|gland]] at the base of your brain. In your teens, other [[@hormones|hormones]] speed things up, then tell the growth plates to finish. Once they turn to solid bone, you stop getting taller.

st.prompt: During which part of the day does your body release the most growth hormone?

Right after lunch

st.reveal: Your body sends out growth hormone in bursts, and the biggest bursts come during deep sleep, especially in the first part of the night. That's one reason sleep matters so much for growing children.

myth: Drinking coffee or tea stunts your growth.
There's no good evidence that caffeine makes children shorter. But caffeine can disturb sleep, and sleep is when most growth hormone is released, so it's still sensible for children to go easy on it.

sec.t:
Growing isn't steady. Babies grow fastest of all. A newborn is about 50 cm long and grows around 25 cm in the first year. That's almost the length of a school ruler in twelve months, though it slows quickly after that.

Through middle childhood, most children grow about 5 or 6 cm a year. Then comes [[@body-growth-spurts|the growth spurt]] of [[@puberty-basics|puberty]], when a child can shoot up 8 to 10 cm in a single year. Girls usually start this spurt earlier, around 10 to 12, and boys a couple of years later. That's why, for a while, many girls in a class are taller than the boys. By the late teens, the growth plates close and height settles.

sec.h: What decides how tall you'll be

sec.t:
On Earth, [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] squashes your spine a little all day. Between each of the small bones in your back sit soft discs, like jam-filled cushions. As you stand and walk, they flatten slightly. At night, lying down, they spring back. That's why you're about a centimetre taller in the morning.

Astronauts on the International Space Station can become up to 3% taller, because there's no [[gravity|gravity]] pressing on their spines. That can mean a few centimetres. NASA designs [[@spacesuits|spacesuits]] with room for this. Once astronauts come back to Earth, their spines settle again within a few months.

The tallest person ever reliably measured was Robert Wadlow, from Illinois in the USA. He reached [[@body-height-limit|2.72 metres]] (8 feet 11 inches) before he died in 1940. His body made far too much growth hormone, and his growth plates never closed.

That's very rare. A doctor checks a child's growth over time by plotting height on a growth chart. A child growing much faster or slower than usual may need tests, and treatment exists for some growth problems. Most differences in height, though, are simply normal. Everyone's [[@bones|bones]] follow their own timetable, and children who are small at ten are often not small at sixteen.

text: Mental health is how you're doing on the inside: how you think, how you feel and how you cope with life. It affects how you sleep, learn, play and get along with people. The World Health Organization describes good mental health as being able to handle the normal stresses of life, learn and work well, and feel part of your community.

Everyone has mental health, just as everyone has physical health. Both go up and down. A bad week after a fight with a friend is normal. When sad, worried or angry feelings stay for weeks and get in the way of everyday life, it may be a mental health condition, and help is available.

st.prompt: The World Health Organization says about half of all mental health conditions start before a certain age. Which age?
st.reveal: About half begin by 14, and most by the mid-twenties. That's why doctors, schools and families now pay attention to how children and teenagers are feeling, and why getting help early makes a difference.

Conditions like depression and anxiety are health problems, linked to the brain, the body and life events. Nobody chooses them, and strong, successful people get them too. Like other health problems, they usually get better with the right support.

sec.h: A body and a mind, wired together
sec.t:
Your feelings come from your brain, which is part of your body. So it makes sense that the body and mind affect each other. Poor sleep can make worries feel bigger. Exercise, sunlight and time with friends often lift people's mood. A frightening event can make the heart race and the stomach churn, which is your [[@stress|stress]] system switching on. Hunger, illness and even a long spell of hot weather can change how people feel.

The most common conditions are anxiety and depression. Anxiety is worry that is too strong or won't switch off. Depression is more than feeling sad. It can make people feel flat, tired and uninterested in things they used to enjoy, for weeks at a time.

If you feel low or worried for a long time, the first step is to tell an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher or a school counsellor. Doctors can help too. Treatment might mean talking regularly with a trained counsellor, learning ways to handle difficult thoughts, and sometimes medicine prescribed by a doctor.

Many countries now run free phone helplines. In India, the government launched Tele-MANAS, on 14416, in 2022. In the USA, people can call or text 988. Both connect callers with trained people who listen. Asking for help is a sensible thing to do, the same as seeing a doctor for a broken arm.

Some everyday habits support mental health for most people. Getting enough [[@sleep-why|sleep]] is one of the biggest. Moving your body, eating regular meals, spending time outdoors and having a few good [[@friendship|friendships]] all help.

So does noticing your feelings and putting them into words. Scientists have found that naming an emotion, even just saying "I feel nervous", can make it a little easier to manage. These habits don't stop hard times from coming. They're more like a good raincoat: they help you get through the weather.

text: Old phones, laptops, televisions, [[@chargers|chargers]] and other gadgets become electronic waste, or e-waste. Some are repaired and sold again. Some are taken apart, and the valuable metals inside, such as gold, copper and silver, are recovered. But a lot is simply thrown away or left forgotten in drawers.

The world threw away about 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, according to a United Nations report. That's enough to fill more than a million and a half large trucks. Only about 22% was properly collected and [[@recycling|recycled]]. India is one of the three biggest producers, after China and the United States.

About half
Almost all of it

st.reveal: The Global E-waste Monitor found only about 22% was documented as properly collected and recycled. The rest was dumped, burned, stored in drawers or handled by informal workers without records.

myth: Most old electronics get recycled.

Worldwide, only about a fifth of e-waste is properly recycled. Much of it sits forgotten in drawers or ends up with informal recyclers who burn wires and use acids, which can harm workers and pollute soil and water.

sec.h: A gold mine in a drawer

sec.t:
In India, most e-waste doesn't go to big factories. It goes to kabadiwalas, the scrap dealers who buy old newspapers and broken gadgets door to door. They sell to markets like Seelampur in [[@delhi|Delhi]], one of the country's biggest informal e-waste hubs, where thousands of workers take devices apart by hand.

These workers keep a lot of metal in use that would otherwise be thrown away. But the methods can be dangerous. Some burn plastic off wires to get the copper, or dip circuit boards in [[acid|acid]] to pull out gold. The smoke and fumes contain lead, mercury and other poisons that harm the workers, often including children, and leak into soil and water.

E-waste contains harmful materials as well as valuable ones. Old TV screens had lead in their glass. Some switches and lamps contain mercury. Lithium [[@batteries-phones|batteries]] can catch fire if crushed in a rubbish truck. Plastics in cases and cables can give off toxic smoke when burned.

That's why e-waste shouldn't go in the normal bin. Dumped in a landfill, it can slowly leak these chemicals into the ground.

India's E-Waste (Management) Rules, first made in 2011 and updated in 2016 and 2022, say that companies that make or sell electronics are responsible for collecting a share back for recycling. This idea is called extended producer responsibility. Authorised recyclers must handle the waste safely and keep records.

In the United States, rules differ from state to state. Some states require makers to pay for recycling, and many shops run take-back schemes for old phones and [[@batteries|batteries]].

The best way to cut e-waste is to make it less often. Repairing a cracked screen or replacing a tired battery can keep a phone going for years. A "right to repair" movement, strong in the United States and Europe, is pushing companies to sell spare parts and share repair manuals. A [[@smartphones|smartphone]] handed down to a younger cousin is one less gadget in a drawer.

text: NavIC is India's own satellite [[navigation|navigation]] system. Like the American GPS, it uses satellites that send out precise time signals. A receiver on the ground, in a phone, ship or truck, picks up those signals and works out where it is.

The difference is size. GPS covers the whole Earth with about 30 satellites. NavIC was designed to cover only India and a zone around 1,500 km beyond its borders, using a planned seven satellites. That smaller job means fewer satellites, placed very high above the Indian Ocean so they always stay in view. The system was built by [[@isro-launch|ISRO]], and the Indian government controls it, so it cannot be switched off by anyone else.

st.prompt: Why does a navigation receiver need signals from at least four satellites, not three?

options.t: The fourth signal lets it correct its own clock
One satellite is always switched off as a backup
Each satellite only works for one compass direction

st.reveal: Three distances are enough to pin down a spot in space, but only if the receiver's clock is perfect. Phone clocks are not, so a fourth signal is used to work out the timing error too.

GPS belongs to the USA and covers the whole planet. NavIC is India's own regional system, covering India and the area around it. Many phones can listen to both, plus Russia's, Europe's and China's systems.

sec.t:
Satellite navigation became part of everyday life in the 1990s and 2000s. Ships, planes, banks, power grids and armies all came to rely on it. Yet the best-known systems belonged to the USA and Russia.

A story often told in India is that during the Kargil conflict in 1999, India asked for detailed GPS data and did not get it. Whatever the exact details, the lesson was clear to planners: a country that leans on someone else's satellites can be left in the dark. India approved its own regional system in 2006.

Indian fishing boats can carry NavIC receivers that show their position and receive messages about storms and sea borders, useful far from mobile phone towers. Trucks, buses and trains use it for tracking. Since 2020, several phone chips can pick up NavIC signals alongside GPS, and the Indian government has pushed phone makers to support it.

Banks, telecom networks and power grids also use its precise timing to keep their computers in step.

NavIC has had real trouble. Its first satellite went up in July 2013. Soon after, atomic clocks on several satellites began to fail, and one launch in 2017 failed when the rocket's nose cone did not open. A new generation began with NVS-01 in 2023, which carried an atomic clock made in India.

In January 2025, ISRO's 100th launch from Sriharikota carried NVS-02, but a valve problem left it stuck in the wrong [[orbit|orbit]]. By July 2026, the government told Parliament that only three satellites were working. That is one short of the four needed for a position fix, so NavIC could provide accurate timing but not standalone positioning. On 30 October 2026, a GSLV rocket carried a new satellite, NVS-03, into orbit. Once it is tested and in place, it should bring the count back to four, with more launches planned. For now, phones in India mostly mix NavIC with GPS and other systems, and users hardly notice.

Several countries now run their own navigation satellites. Russia has GLONASS, Europe has Galileo and China has BeiDou. Japan, like India, has a regional system. A modern phone may listen to dozens of satellites from four or five systems at once, picking whichever give the cleanest signals. That is one reason a [[@maps-digital|map app]] can find you on a narrow lane in Old Delhi or a Chicago street lined with skyscrapers.

text: A particle accelerator is a machine that speeds up tiny particles, such as [[electron|electrons]], [[proton|protons]] or the centres of atoms, using electric and magnetic forces. It gives them a lot of energy and then aims them at a target or at each other.

Scientists use the biggest accelerators to smash particles together and study what comes flying out. That tells them what matter is made of at the smallest scale. But accelerators also have everyday jobs. Hospitals use small ones to treat cancer, and factories use them to make computer chips. If you're old enough to remember a fat, old box TV, that was a tiny accelerator too. It fired a beam of electrons at the screen to make the picture.

st.reveal: There are tens of thousands of small accelerators at work. Many in hospitals make beams that treat cancer, and others in factories help make computer chips or sterilise medical equipment. Only a few are giant research machines like the LHC.

d.try: Rub a balloon on your hair or a woolly jumper, then hold it close to a thin stream of water from a tap. The stream bends towards the balloon. The balloon's electric charge is pulling on the water, which is the same kind of force accelerators use to push particles faster and faster.
myth: The Large Hadron Collider could make a black hole that swallows the Earth.

Scientists checked this carefully before it was switched on. Cosmic rays from space hit Earth and the Moon with even more energy all the time, and they have never made a dangerous black hole. The LHC has run for years without any problem of this kind.

sec.t:
Particles like protons and electrons carry an electric charge. That means electric fields can push them, the same way a charged balloon can pull your hair. Each push adds a bit more speed.

A linear accelerator lines up many pushing sections in a straight tube, and particles get faster down its length. A circular one sends them around a ring, giving them a push each lap. Powerful [[@magnets-how|magnets]] bend their path so they stay on the circle. Inside the tubes, the air is pumped out so the particles don't crash into air [[molecule|molecules]].

The biggest accelerator in the world is the Large Hadron Collider, or LHC, run by CERN near Geneva. Its ring is about 27 km around and sits about 100 m underground, crossing the border between [[@switzerland|Switzerland]] and France.

Two beams of protons travel in opposite directions, each going at more than 99.9999 per cent of the speed of light. They loop around the ring about 11,000 times a second. At four points, the beams cross and protons collide. Huge detectors, some as tall as an eight-storey building, record the spray of new particles.

The magnets that steer the beams are cooled with liquid helium to about minus 271 °C, colder than outer space. At that temperature, their wires carry electricity with no resistance.

{{story:einstein}}

On 4 July 2012, scientists at CERN announced that they had found a new particle, the Higgs boson. Physicists had predicted it nearly 50 years earlier. It is linked to a field that gives other basic particles their mass.

Finding it took thousands of scientists from dozens of countries, including India. Indian physicists have helped build and run two of the LHC's big detectors, and India became an associate member of CERN in 2017.

sec.h: Accelerators in India and the US
sec.t:
India has accelerators of its own. At Indore, the Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology runs two rings called Indus-1 and Indus-2. As electrons whizz around them, they give off very bright light, including [[@x-rays|X-rays]], which scientists use to study materials, medicines and even ancient objects.

The United States has big accelerator labs too. Fermilab, near Chicago, ran the Tevatron, the world's most powerful collider until the LHC took over. At Stanford in California, SLAC has a straight accelerator about 3 km long.

Most accelerators are small. In hospitals, machines called linacs, short for linear accelerators, fire electron beams that make X-rays to destroy cancer cells. They are carefully aimed so healthy tissue is spared as much as possible.

Factories use accelerators to plant tiny amounts of other [[element|elements]] into silicon when making chips. Others kill germs on medical tools and some foods. Ernest Lawrence's first cyclotron, a circular accelerator built in California around 1930 to 1931, was small enough to hold in your hand. The LHC is the same idea, made wide enough to circle a city.

text: Vikram Sarabhai was the scientist who started India's space programme. In the 1960s he persuaded the government that a poor, newly independent country should still build rockets and satellites, because they could help with farming, weather, communication and education.

He founded the group that became ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, and set up its [[@launch-sites|first launch site]] at Thumba in [[@kerala|Kerala]]. He also started research laboratories, a famous business school and [[textile|textile]] research centres. He died young, at 52, but the space agency he planned has since sent missions to the Moon and Mars.

st.prompt: Why did Sarabhai choose Thumba, a fishing village near Thiruvananthapuram, for India's first rocket launches?

options.t: It lies almost on the Earth's magnetic equator
It is the highest point in India
It is the furthest place from the sea

st.reveal: The Earth's magnetic equator passes very close to Thumba. Scientists wanted to study the upper air there, where the Earth's magnetic field creates unusual effects. The launch site also faced the sea, so spent rockets could fall safely into the water.

The first rocket launched from Thumba was an American-made Nike-Apache. Countries including the United States, France and the Soviet Union helped India start out. Indian engineers learned quickly and soon built their own sounding rockets, called Rohini.

sec.t:
Sarabhai was born in 1919 into a wealthy family of mill owners in [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]]. The house was full of visitors, including leaders of the freedom movement and the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]].

He studied in Gujarat and at Cambridge. During the Second World War he returned to India and worked in Bangalore with C. V. Raman, studying cosmic rays, the fast particles that rain down on the Earth from space. There he met [[@homi-bhabha|Homi Bhabha]], who would become a lifelong friend. Back at Cambridge he completed his doctorate in 1947.

That same year, aged 28, he founded the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad. It began in a few rooms of a college and is now one of India's leading space science centres.

After the Soviet Union launched [[@sputnik|Sputnik]] in 1957, Sarabhai argued that India needed a space programme of its own. In 1962 the government set up a space research committee, with him in charge.

He chose Thumba, [[@people-fishing-villages|a fishing village]] near Thiruvananthapuram, because it lies almost on the Earth's magnetic [[equator|equator]]. The local bishop and the village community agreed to give up the land, including the Church of St Mary Magdalene. The church became an office and workshop. Rocket parts were carried to the launch pad on [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]] and bullock carts. A photograph of a young technician cycling with a rocket nose cone on his carrier is now one of the best-known pictures in Indian science.

On 21 November 1963, a small American rocket lifted off from Thumba. Sarabhai gathered a team of young engineers around him, and one of those who grew up in his programme was [[@apj-kalam|A. P. J. Abdul Kalam]]. The old church is now a space museum.

{{story:rockets-how}}

Sarabhai believed space technology should solve problems on the ground. He planned a satellite to beam [[@television-invented|educational television]] to villages that had never had TV. This became the Satellite Instructional Television Experiment of 1975–76, which used an American satellite to reach about 2,400 villages with programmes on farming, health and hygiene. It changed the story of [[@tv-india|television in India]].

He also pushed India to build its own satellites. The first, Aryabhata, went up in 1975, four years after his death.

Sarabhai co-founded the Indian Institute of Management in Ahmedabad and set up a research group to help the textile mills of Gujarat. His wife, Mrinalini Sarabhai, was a classical dancer who founded the Darpana Academy of Performing Arts.

He died in his sleep at Kovalam, near Thumba, in December 1971. The rocket centre at Thiruvananthapuram is now the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre. When ISRO sent its lander towards the Moon on [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-2]] in 2019, it named the lander Vikram. The lander that touched down safely near the Moon's south pole in 2023 carried the same name.

text: The Cold War was a long rivalry, from about 1947 to 1991, between the United States and the Soviet Union, a communist country centred on Russia. Both had been allies in the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], but they had very different ideas about how countries should be run.

The USA believed in elections and private businesses. The Soviet Union was ruled by a single Communist Party, which controlled the [[economy|economy]]. Each side feared the other would spread its system across the world. They never fought each other directly, because both had nuclear weapons and a war could have destroyed them both. Instead they competed in almost everything else.

st.reveal: The drills were called "duck and cover", and a cartoon turtle called Bert taught them in a 1951 film. The desks would not have helped much in a real nuclear attack, but the drills show how afraid people were.

myth: The Cold War was called "cold" because it was fought in snowy places.
It was "cold" because the two superpowers never fought each other directly in a "hot" war. Instead they competed through spying, weapons, space and wars fought by other countries.

sec.t:
After 1945, Soviet troops stayed in the countries of eastern Europe they had freed from [[@germany|Germany]], and communist governments took charge there. In 1946, Britain's Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had come down across Europe.

The USA and western European countries formed a military alliance, NATO, in 1949. The Soviet Union and its allies formed the Warsaw Pact in 1955. Germany itself was split in two, and later its old capital was divided by the [[@berlin-wall|Berlin Wall]].

The USA dropped the first atomic bombs in 1945. The Soviet Union tested its own in 1949. Both sides then built thousands of ever more powerful weapons, a contest called the arms race.

The same science powered new [[@nuclear-power|nuclear power]] stations, but the weapons made people everywhere nervous. Some American families built fallout shelters in their gardens, stocked with tinned food and water. Both sides also tested huge bombs in deserts, on remote islands and underground.

The scariest moment came in October 1962. The USA discovered that the Soviet Union was secretly placing nuclear missiles in Cuba, only about 150 km from Florida. US President John F. Kennedy surrounded Cuba with navy ships. For thirteen days, the world waited.

Finally, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. Secretly, the USA agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey. Afterwards, the two sides set up a direct hotline so their leaders could talk quickly in a crisis.

Rockets that could carry bombs could also carry [[@satellites-help|satellites]]. In 1957 the Soviet Union launched [[@sputnik|Sputnik]], the first satellite. Americans were shocked, and the [[@space-race|space race]] began. It ended with Americans walking on the Moon in 1969.

{{story:sputnik}}

Although the superpowers avoided fighting each other, they backed opposite sides in wars elsewhere, including Korea from 1950 to 1953, [[@vietnam|Vietnam]] and Afghanistan. Millions of people died in these conflicts.

India did not want to join either camp. [[@nehru|Nehru]] helped found the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961, with leaders from Egypt, Yugoslavia, Indonesia and Ghana. India took help from both sides: American wheat and Soviet steel plants. In 1971, India signed a friendship [[treaty|treaty]] with the Soviet Union, and the two countries stayed close for years.

In the 1980s, the Soviet economy was struggling. A new leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, allowed more freedom of speech and tried to reform the system. Across eastern Europe, people protested peacefully against their governments. On 9 November 1989, the Berlin Wall opened.

In 1991, the Soviet Union split into 15 separate countries, the largest being [[@russia|Russia]]. The Cold War was over. The two sides still had thousands of nuclear weapons, but the fear of a sudden world-ending war began to fade.

text: Ahmedabad, in Gujarat, was named India's first World Heritage City by UNESCO in 2017. The honour is for its old walled city, on the east bank of the Sabarmati river. It still has narrow lanes, gated neighbourhoods called pols, carved wooden houses and centuries-old mosques and temples.

What makes it special is that the old city is not a museum. Families still live in the pols, shops still open in the morning, and temples and mosques are still in daily use. Ahmedabad is also where [[@gandhi-south-africa|Gandhi]] lived and planned much of the freedom struggle, and it was one of India's great [[textile|textile]] cities.

st.reveal: A pol is a cluster of houses along narrow lanes, usually entered through a gateway. Families living there often shared a profession, a community or a temple, and the gate could be shut at night for safety.

myth: Gandhi lived in Ahmedabad's Sabarmati Ashram for most of his life.
He lived there for about 13 years, from 1917 to 1930. He left on the Salt March in 1930 and vowed not to return until India was free. He never lived there again.

sec.h: A city of gates and lanes
sec.t:
Sultan Ahmad Shah founded the city in 1411 and named it after himself. It grew into a busy trading centre, famous for cloth, and was surrounded by walls with about a dozen gates. Many of the gates still stand, though the walls have mostly gone.

Inside the old city are hundreds of pols. Each is a cluster of houses along winding lanes, often entered through a single gateway. Houses have carved wooden balconies, brackets and doors, with courtyards open to the sky that let in light and catch rainwater. Many pols have a chabutro, a tall, decorated bird-feeding tower, where families leave grain for birds every day.

In 1917, [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] set up an ashram on the banks of the Sabarmati. He lived there with his wife Kasturba and his followers, spinning cotton, farming and teaching. He urged people to spin and wear [[@khadi|khadi]], handspun cloth, instead of buying factory cloth from Britain.

On 12 March 1930, Gandhi and 78 followers left the ashram on the [[@salt-march|Salt March]] to Dandi, about 385 km away on the coast, to make salt against British law. He vowed not to return until India was free, and he never lived there again. Today the ashram is a museum, with his simple room and spinning wheel.

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, Ahmedabad built dozens of cotton mills and became known as the "Manchester of the East", after the English mill city. Its long tradition of [[@textiles-india|textiles]] is shown in the Calico Museum, one of India's finest cloth collections.

Every January, during [[@pop-kites-patang|Uttarayan]], the whole city climbs onto its rooftops to fly kites. The sky fills with thousands of them, and people try to cut each other's strings. At night, food streets serve dhokla, khandvi, fafda and other [[@gujarati-food|Gujarati snacks]]. Modern Ahmedabad has grown far beyond the old walls, with [[@indian-architecture-modern|famous buildings]] by architects like Louis Kahn and Le Corbusier. Yet the city's identity still starts in those narrow lanes behind the old gates.

text: In the hills of [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], in north-east India, Khasi and Jaintia villagers grow bridges from the roots of a tree called the rubber fig. This tree sends long roots down from its branches and trunk. Builders guide these young roots across a stream, often along a hollow bamboo or palm trunk, until they reach the far bank and root into the soil.

Over the years, more roots are added, twisted and woven together. Stones fill the gaps to make a walkway. After about 15 years or more, people can cross. The bridge keeps growing for as long as the tree lives, and some are thought to be well over 100 years old.

st.prompt: Why do living root bridges get stronger as they age, while wooden bridges get weaker?

options.t: The roots are alive, so they keep growing thicker and fusing together
