sec.t:
This region is wet. [[@india-wonder-cherrapunji|Cherrapunji]] and nearby Mawsynram are among the rainiest places on Earth, with more than 11 metres of rain in a year. Stacked up, that much water would rise higher than a three-storey house. In the [[monsoon|monsoon]], quiet streams turn into roaring rivers.

A wooden bridge rots in a few years in such damp. Steel rusts, and carrying it up steep jungle paths is hard. A living bridge needs no factory and no lorry. It just needs a tree, time and patient hands. The roots also grip the soil of steep banks, so a root bridge helps stop the stream from washing the path away.

The most famous root bridge is near the village of Nongriat, below Tyrna. It has two levels, one root bridge above another, crossing the same stream. Visitors reach it by climbing down thousands of stone steps through the forest, and then, harder, climbing back up.

Some villages have also grown root ladders up cliffs and root platforms along slopes. The bridges are part of a whole way of life in which forests, streams and farms are looked after together.

sec.h: A design the world is studying
sec.t:
Engineers usually build [[@bridges|bridges]] that are strongest on the day they open and slowly wear out. A root bridge does the opposite. Researchers from Germany studied dozens of Meghalaya's bridges and published their findings in 2019. They are interested in using living plants in city buildings, an idea some architects call "tree [[architecture|architecture]]".

Local groups have counted root bridges in more than 70 villages. In 2022, India added them to [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO]]'s tentative list of World Heritage Sites, the first step towards full recognition.

The bridges now attract thousands of tourists, which brings money to villages but also litter and wear. Too many feet can damage young roots, and some villages have started charging small fees and limiting crowds.

There is another worry. As roads and concrete bridges arrive, fewer young people learn the old skill. So some communities and local groups now teach children how to start and care for a new bridge. The trees are part of something bigger. The hills around them hold forests full of frogs, orchids and birds found almost nowhere else, as rich in places as the great [[@rainforests|rainforests]] near the [[equator|equator]].

text: Mumbai's suburban railway carries around 60 to 75 lakh passenger trips on a typical weekday, more than the whole population of many countries. It does it with frequent trains, long trains, separate fast and slow tracks, and passengers who pack in far beyond normal limits.

At rush hour, trains on the busiest lines can arrive every three or four minutes. Each has 12 or 15 coaches. A 12-coach train is rated for about 2,000 passengers, but during the morning and evening peaks it often carries more than 4,500. People hang from doorways and squeeze into every gap. The system works, but at a huge cost in comfort and safety.

st.reveal: Mumbai is squeezed between the sea and a creek, stretching north from its old island tip. Homes are mostly in the north and many offices in the south, so huge numbers of people travel the same direction along three main rail corridors every morning.

sec.h: A city shaped like a finger
sec.t:
[[@mumbai|Mumbai]] is a long, narrow city, squeezed between the Arabian Sea and Thane Creek. Its old business centre is at the southern tip. Many people live in the northern suburbs and travel south every morning.

There is only so much land, so three main railway corridors carry most of these journeys: the Western line, the Central line and the Harbour line. Roads are crowded too, and a car journey can take two or three times as long at rush hour. For millions of people, the local train is the fastest and cheapest way to work. A monthly season ticket can cost less than a single taxi ride across the city.

Railway planners measure crowding in people per square metre. On a comfortable train, it might be four. In Mumbai at peak times, it can reach 14 to 16, called super dense crush load. That's like fitting a whole cricket team, plus a few substitutes, inside a square of tape one metre on each side.

The crowding is dangerous. People fall from open doorways or are hit while crossing tracks. In the 2000s, thousands of people died on Mumbai's tracks every year. Deaths have fallen since, thanks to new bridges, fences and safety campaigns, but the problem is not solved. New trains with automatic closing doors are being added.

sec.h: More than a century of trains
sec.t:
India's first passenger train ran in Mumbai, then called Bombay, on 16 April 1853, from Bori Bunder to Thane, about 34 km. The [[@hist-first-train-india|first train]] was pulled by steam engines. On 3 February 1925, the first electric local train ran from Victoria Terminus to Kurla.

The network has grown ever since, with new lines, longer trains and air-conditioned locals. Central Railway alone ran about 1,800 suburban services a day in 2026.

Mumbai is building new metro lines, more local trains and new railway tracks to spread the crowd. The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link and coastal roads add other routes. Planners hope these will make the morning trip less of a squeeze.

But the local train remains Mumbai's heartbeat. On a typical morning, the trains carry office workers, students, vendors, musicians and fishermen with baskets. People play cards, sing bhajans, chop vegetables for dinner and share news. And the [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawalas]] ride alongside them, their lunchboxes stacked in crates, depending on the same trains to get every lunch there on time.

text: The Bhagavad Gita, meaning "Song of the Lord", is a Hindu [[scripture|scripture]] of 700 verses in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. It is part of the great epic the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], but it is so widely read that it is often printed as a book on its own.

It is a conversation on a battlefield between Prince Arjuna and Krishna, who is acting as his charioteer. Many Hindus worship Krishna as a form of the god Vishnu. Arjuna doesn't want to fight a war against his own cousins, teachers and elders. Krishna answers his doubts with teachings about duty, action, the soul and devotion to God. For many Hindus, the Gita is one of the most sacred and loved texts.

st.prompt: Where does the conversation in the Bhagavad Gita take place?

options.t: On a battlefield, just before a great war begins
In a quiet forest hermitage
In a royal palace during a feast

st.reveal: The Gita is set on the field of Kurukshetra, between two armies of cousins ready to fight. Arjuna asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive between the armies, and on seeing his relatives and teachers on the other side, he loses heart. The whole Gita is Krishna's reply.

n.certNote: Scholars agree the Gita is part of the Mahabharata, but they disagree about when it was composed, with estimates ranging from about the 5th century BCE to the 2nd century CE. People also read its message in very different ways.

sec.t:
The Mahabharata tells of a long feud between two branches of a royal family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. Talks fail, and both sides gather huge armies at Kurukshetra, in what is now Haryana.

Just before the battle, Arjuna, the finest archer of the Pandavas, asks Krishna to drive his chariot into the middle. He sees grandfathers, teachers and cousins on the other side. His hands shake and his bow slips. He says he would rather lose than kill his own family. The rest of the Gita is Krishna's answer over 18 chapters.

For more than a thousand years, teachers have written commentaries explaining the Gita, and they don't all agree. Adi Shankara, in about the 8th century, stressed knowledge. Later teachers like Ramanuja stressed devotion. In the 13th century, the saint Dnyaneshwar explained it in Marathi, so ordinary people could understand it.

In modern times, Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote a long book on the Gita while in prison in Mandalay, reading it as a call to action. [[@gandhi|Gandhi]], who called it his guide, read the battle as a picture of the struggle between good and evil inside every person, and found in it support for non-violence. Others read the battle more literally. These different readings are part of the Gita's long life.

In 1785, Charles Wilkins, who worked for the East India Company, published the first English translation. Soon it was read in Europe and America. The American writers Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau admired it. [[@swami-vivekananda|Swami Vivekananda]] spoke about its ideas during his visit to America in the 1890s.

Today the Gita has been translated into many languages. When the scientist Robert Oppenheimer watched the first atomic bomb test in 1945, he later said a line from the Gita came into his mind. Its questions about duty and fear speak to people far beyond India.

Many Hindu families keep a copy at home, and some recite a few verses every day. Gita Jayanti, celebrated in the month of Margashirsha, marks the day the teachings are believed to have been given. At Kurukshetra, pilgrims visit Jyotisar, where tradition says Krishna spoke to Arjuna.

People who aren't Hindu read the Gita too, as poetry, [[philosophy|philosophy]] or history. Some study it in school, others in a quiet moment before an exam. The opening question, what should I do when doing the right thing feels hard, is one almost everyone faces.

text: There is no single hardest language. How hard a language is depends on where you start. For an English speaker, Dutch or Spanish is fairly easy, because they share many words and grammar ideas. Japanese, Arabic, Korean and Mandarin Chinese are much harder, because almost everything is different: the sounds, the grammar and the writing.

For a child growing up in Tamil Nadu, Malayalam might feel easy and English harder. For a child in Beijing, Cantonese might be easier than English. Every human baby can learn any language. Difficulty only appears when you learn later, and it comes from distance: how far the new language is from the ones you already know.

sec.t:
The US Foreign Service Institute trains diplomats in more than 60 languages. Over many years, it has estimated how long English-speaking adults take to reach good working ability.

Spanish, French, Italian and Dutch are in the easiest group, about 24 to 30 weeks of full-time classes. German takes about 36 weeks. Hindi, Bengali, Russian and many others take about 44 weeks. The hardest group, about 88 weeks, includes Arabic, Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean and Japanese. That is almost two years of study, all day, every working day.

Some languages change words a lot. In Finnish and Hungarian, a noun can take more than a dozen different forms, depending on its job in a sentence. Russian nouns change endings in six ways. In Hindi, verbs change for whether the speaker is a man or a woman: *main jaata hoon* and *main jaati hoon* both mean "I go".

Some languages pack long ideas into a single word. In Turkish or in languages of the Arctic, one word can say what English needs a whole sentence for. And word order can flip: Japanese, Korean, Hindi and Tamil usually put the verb at the end.

sec.h: Easy for some, hard for others
sec.t:
India shows how much starting point matters. Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati and Bengali share many words and grammar patterns, because they all grew from older Sanskrit-related languages. A Marathi speaker can often understand some Hindi without lessons.

Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to a different family, the Dravidian languages. They have their own scripts and grammar. A Hindi speaker learning Tamil faces a bigger jump. Yet millions of Indians grow up speaking three or four [[@languages-india|languages]], switching between them in a single conversation.

Babies are born able to hear the sounds of all human languages. By around their first birthday, they start tuning in to the sounds they hear most. Young children learn grammar by listening and playing, without lessons. Adults are better at study and memory, but young children usually end up with the most natural accent.

So the hardest language might simply be the one you start latest. Scientists who study the [[@bilingual-brain|bilingual brain]] say that learning any second language can make it easier to learn a third, and it may keep the brain sharper as you age. And if you find spoken languages hard, spare a thought for people who learn [[@whistled-languages|whistled languages]], which turn words into tunes that carry across mountain valleys.

text: Rock layers are like pages in Earth's diary, with the oldest at the bottom. At the Grand Canyon, very old rock sits right under much younger rock, and about 1.2 billion years of pages are missing.
The rock was not lost by magic. It was probably worn away by [[erosion|erosion]] over a very long time. The big question is what lifted the land up so it could be worn down.

quiz.prompt: If land is pushed slowly upwards for millions of years, what happens to the rock on top?

options.t: Rain, rivers and wind wear it away
It piles up into thicker and thicker layers
It stays exactly the same forever

quiz.reveal: High land gets worn down by weather and running water, and the bits are carried off to the sea. Layers only pile up where land is low or underwater. So if a continent is lifted for a very long time, its rock record gets erased instead of written.

myth: Rock layers always build up steadily, so every year of Earth's history is stored somewhere in a canyon wall.
Rock layers are more like a diary with many pages ripped out. Layers form only where sediment settles, and they can later be worn away. Most places on Earth keep only a patchy record.
facts: 11 November 2026 (Live Science), study in Nature, 4 November 2026

sec.t:
On 11 November 2026, Live Science reported a new study published in the journal Nature on 4 November. Two [[geologist|geologists]], Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong in Australia, used a computer model of how Earth's insides move over hundreds of millions of years.

Their model suggests that slow, hot currents in the [[mantle|mantle]], the thick layer under Earth's crust, pushed parts of ancient continents upwards. Wind, rain and rivers then scraped those high lands down. Around 540 million years ago, the same regions began to sink, and new layers started piling up on top.

The [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] is about 1.8 km deep at its deepest. The Colorado River cut it, exposing layer after layer like a sliced cake.

Near the bottom lie dark, twisted rocks about 1.7 billion years old, some of the [[@rocks-oldest|oldest rocks]] you can see in North America. Directly above them are flat layers of sandstone only about 500 million years old. The line where they meet is called the Great Unconformity. "Unconformity" is a geologist's word for a break in the record.

The timing is interesting. Just after the gap ends, life on Earth suddenly became far more varied in the [[@cambrian|Cambrian]] period. Some scientists think minerals washed off the eroding land into the sea may have helped.

Other teams have different ideas. Some think enormous [[glacier|glaciers]], during times when much of Earth was covered in ice, ground the rock away. In August 2026, a team at the University of Southampton suggested that a giant cliff once stretched across ancient North America and slowly ate its way backwards as it eroded. The Wollongong team agrees glaciers probably helped, but says the land had to be lifted first.

Geologists will test the new model against more places where the gap appears, from Scandinavia to China. Each answer helps explain how Earth's surface and the life on it changed together.
